Game: This picture puts a triangle on each side of a regular shape and joins the new points.
How to play: Choose how many sides, drag the purple dot to turn the picture, and press Check the claim to read what happens.
Look for the math

Why do the tips of the triangles make another regular polygon, and how does that answer a question about dots on a triangular grid? The construction is David Radcliffe's solution to a question from James Tanton; the applet and its page are by Alexander Bogomolny (copyright 1996–2018). The logic test checked every setting the applet offers, from 3 to 30 sides. The Java applet had only the sides spinner; the turning dot and Check button here are reading aids, not extra rules.

A smaller copy every time

Number the corners of a regular N-gon V[0], V[1], ... around a centre O. An equilateral triangle on the side from V[i] to V[i+1] has its tip at U[i] = V[i] + rot60(V[i+1] - V[i]), where rot60 is a turn through 60°. Rotating the whole picture by 2π/N carries each side to the next, so it carries each tip to the next tip: the tips are equally spaced on a circle and form a regular N-gon.

U[i] = λ V[i], where λ = 1 + eiπ/3(e2πi/N - 1) and |λ| = |cos(π/N) - √3 sin(π/N)| = |2 cos(π/N + π/3)|.

The test measured the tips for every N from 3 to 30: they agree with this formula and are always equally spaced. For N = 3 the factor is 1 (a same-size triangle turned halfway round); for N = 6 it is 0 (all six tips fall on the centre). For every other N in the range it is strictly between 0 and 1, so the new polygon is smaller. Those two exceptions are exactly the ones the page names.

Why the grid keeps the new points

Take the grid made by the vectors u = (1,0) and v = (1/2, √3/2). Its nodes are m u + n v with whole numbers m, n — the points called Eisenstein integers. A turn of 60° about a node sends u to v and v to v - u, so (m,n) becomes (-n, m+n): whole numbers stay whole numbers. The same is true for a turn the other way. Hence a segment between any two grid nodes is the base of exactly two equilateral triangles whose tips are also grid nodes; the test checked all 288 non-zero pairs with coordinates from −8 to 8 in both directions.

No square in the grid

If a square with grid-node corners existed, the construction would give a smaller square, still with grid-node corners. Applying it again gives a smaller one, and another, for ever. There is no infinite strictly shrinking chain of shapes with whole-number coordinates, so no such square exists. This is infinite descent. The same argument rules out a grid-node regular N-gon for every N except 3 and 6, where the copy is not smaller. The applet draws the same figure for 3 and 6 sides so you can see why those two escape.

A second way to shrink

Radcliffe also noted that for corners a, b, c, ... the points a + c - b, b + d - c, ... make a smaller regular N-gon. For a regular N-gon centred at O each new point is (2 cos(2π/N) - 1) a, so its size is multiplied by |2 cos(2π/N) - 1|. The test checked every N from 3 to 30: that factor is below 1 except at N = 3 (factor 2), N = 4 (factor 1, a same-size square turned halfway round) and N = 6 (factor 0). Notice that N = 4 is an exception for this second construction but not for the triangle construction the applet draws, where the factor is about 0.52.

Try 4 sides and press Check the claim: the smaller square is why a square cannot sit on the grid. Then try 6 and 3 sides to see the two exceptions.
